demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, a specific sense of danger from strangers is hard to reconcile unless there is additional trauma history not represented here. The other threat items reflect generalized hypervigilance, but this item implies an interpersonal-danger context that is not supported by the trauma type or by any trigger, memory, appraisal, or strategy items.

issues.item: Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, this threat profile is hard to reconcile clinically: all selected items imply persistent fear of immediate external physical danger, which fits assault/combat more than bereavement trauma. In isolation, bereavement-related PTSD can involve arousal, but a purely danger-scanning threat node without any accompanying memory, trigger, appraisal, or strategy content linking the threat to reminders of the loved one's death is not coherent here. This is also difficult to square with the formulation, which specifies no active edges; the threat items strongly imply linkage to triggers or trauma reminders, yet no such connected content is present.

vignette: The rain had come down in sheets that October evening, turning the interstate into a slick, shimmering black mirror. Linh was three hours into her shift at the metro desk when the call came. Her younger brother's sedan had lost traction on the overpass, flipping twice before coming to rest against a concrete median. By the time she reached the hospital, the monitors had gone still, leaving only heavy silence and the crumpled fabric of the driver's seat she had once shared with him. The suddenness of it-the lack of warning, the violent stillness that followed the screech of tires-rewired something in her. She could not relax, even when she knew she was in a safe place. Her apartment deadbolt clicked shut, the blinds were drawn, yet her eyes kept tracking the hallway. She found herself superalert, constantly watchful, always on guard, waiting for the next collapse or the next sudden impact. Alongside that unyielding readiness came strong negative feelings: fear, horror, anger, guilt, shame. When the memory of the wet asphalt flashed behind her eyes, fear would pool in her stomach. Later, staring at his unreturned voicemail, horror tightened her throat. She replayed the morning again and again, dissecting every word of their rushed goodbye, convinced that if she had only spoken differently, he would still be alive. A sharp, persistent anger followed her through the newsroom, flaring at careless drivers, at the weather forecasts, at the world for moving forward. Her work as a journalist became a landscape of retreat. The fluorescent lights of the press room usually hummed with productive energy, but to Linh they now felt like the strobing warning lights of an incoming crisis. She began taking the service staircase down to the street level, avoiding the main lobby where reporters would gather around desks, phones ringing like sirens. That sharp crack of a dropped stack of copy on a colleague's desk last spring sent her heart hammering against her ribs, her vision narrowing until she had to step outside and press her palms against the cool brick wall until the ringing in her ears faded. She stopped covering the emergency beat altogether, though the truth was she could no longer sit in the back of an ambulance or watch flashing red lights sweep across her windows. The constant bracing drained the warmth from her marriage; her ex-husband, David, eventually said he could not reach her, that she was always halfway out the door. They divorced, and she let it go, convinced that keeping everyone at a distance was the only way to prevent another irreversible loss. At thirty-one years old, Linh is sitting in a clinician's office for the first time. She cannot sleep through the night, wakes with her muscles coiled, and finds herself scanning every crowded room as she walks through downtown. What finally brought her here was the exhaustion of perpetually waiting for the next sudden break. She is afraid that the relentless tension in her chest will never fully unwind, that she will forever be braced. What she is hoping for, quietly, is just to sit in a quiet room and let her shoulders finally drop, to feel safe in the rhythm of an unbroken day.
